metrics.precedent_match: Exact match to the GM method, and checked by reproduction. Using the current Home Office outcomes open-data files, I recomputed all 9 GM values (19.25, 13.87, 9.58, 8.76, 9.22, 8.36, 9.22, 10.72, 12.82) exactly. The formula is: sum of column 'Outcomes for offences that were recorded in the quarter' for Outcome Groups Charged/Summonsed (type 1), Out-of-court (formal) (types 2, 3, 6), Out-of-court (informal) (types 7, 8) and Taken into consideration (type 4), divided by the sum of the same column over ALL outcome rows, including 'Not yet assigned an outcome'. That denominator equals all police recorded crime excluding fraud (FY2025-26 = 59,558, identical to ONS PFA Table P1). Two alternatives did not reproduce GM: closed-in-quarter numerator over recorded, and closed over closed. Applied to Force Name 'Durham'.
metrics.caveats: This is an ALL-CRIME positive-outcome rate, not violent-crime-specific as Mandate's definition requires, hence 'estimated' (same treatment as GM). Geography is the Durham Constabulary force area (County Durham + Darlington). The Home Office outcomes open data has no CSP or local-authority split, so no council-area series exists in this source. Outcome 22 (diversionary/educational activity, from April 2019) is excluded, as in GM. Durham assigned 411 to 882 outcome-22 disposals a year from FY2019-20 (Durham's Checkpoint deferred-prosecution scheme is the likely main driver, unverified). Including them would add about 0.6 to 1.6 points, so Durham's post-2019 fall in out-of-court disposals partly reflects reclassification into outcome 22. The latest year is provisional: FY2025-26 still had 3,914 offences (6.6%) 'not yet assigned an outcome', and it will rise on revision. GM's series stops at FY2024-25. The steep fall from FY2015-16 to FY2017-18 coincides with recorded crime rising from 36k to 61k as recording practice tightened, so the denominator effect is large.

metrics.precedent_match: NOT an exact match to GM, and it cannot be. GM's 7.35 is GMFRS's own internal KPI: the mean response to 'life risk' incidents (dwelling, high-rise and building fires, RTCs, chemical incidents, special services, water rescue), timed from call receipt at North West Fire Control. CDDFRS publishes no equivalent life-risk composite. Its public reporting, including Combined Fire Authority 'National Performance' papers, benchmarks against the Home Office FIRE1001 'response time to fires' statistics, and its local standard is a percent-within-time measure for accidental dwelling fires (8 min on 70%, 11 min on 90%). So I used the closest reproducible national measure: Home Office FIRE1001 mean total response time (call to first appliance in attendance) to PRIMARY fires for the County Durham and Darlington FRA. The dwelling-fire figure is in each row's notes in case the founder prefers it. GM can be recomputed on the same basis from the same table: FIRE1001 GM FY2022-23 is primary 7.22 min and dwellings 6.65 min, versus the 7.35 life-risk figure on file. If cross-jurisdiction comparability matters, the GM row should be supplemented or replaced with the FIRE1001 series rather than compared against this one.
metrics.caveats: These are MEANS, not the median Mandate's definition asks for. The Home Office publishes no medians by FRA; FIRE1004 one-minute bands exist but a median read from bands would be a further derivation. They cover fire-service response to primary fires, not police priority-one or ambulance calls. Geography is the FRA covering County Durham AND Darlington; the council does not run the fire service. FIRE1001 values are revised in later releases. I used the current table (published 22 July 2026, data cut 12 May 2026), so older printed figures may differ by a few seconds. The CFA paper on Wayback quotes 9 min 13 sec for YE Mar 2023, but that is the England average, not CDDFRS. I opened FIRE1005 (non-fire incidents, including RTCs) but did not combine it, to avoid building a synthetic life-risk composite. Status is 'estimated' because a mean stands in for a median and the concept differs from GM's life-risk KPI. Note that GM's 7.35 is also a mean but was imported as 'government', an inconsistency worth reviewing.

metrics.unavailable_reason: No measured, dated length of protected or dedicated cycle lanes and trails for County Durham was found. Searched: (1) The council's Strategic Cycling and Walking Delivery Plan 2019-2029 (Evidence Base, Action Plan, and Review of the 2012-15 strategy). These give no network length. The only length mentioned is the single new 2-mile Locomotion Way (2012-15), and the action plan commits to auditing and recording the network rather than reporting its length. (2) The council's 'Where to cycle' page, which says 'County Durham has 543km of bridleways, 45km of byways and over 150km of railway paths', with cycle lanes described only as 'a growing number'. That is a different concept. Bridleways and byways are public rights of way shared with horses and vehicles, often unsurfaced, not dedicated bike infrastructure. The railway-paths figure is a lower bound ('over 150km', about 93 miles) of off-road trails only, excludes on-road protected lanes, and is undated: identical text appears in the Wayback capture of 30 January 2023 and the live page in October 2026, so it supports no time series. (3) Town LCWIPs, which give planned networks, not built lengths. (4) Open data: data.gov.uk CKAN shows no Durham cycle-network dataset. DataMill North, where Durham publishes rights-of-way and adopted-highways layers, blocked access with a Cloudflare challenge, so a cycle layer there could not be checked. (5) No DfT or Sustrans statistic gives cycle lane length by LA. An OpenStreetMap measurement would not be the jurisdiction's own data. If the founder wants a point value, the only defensible option is a single flagged 'railway paths >150 km (93 mi), undated' with status estimated. I recommend against it.
metrics.caveats: Possible future source: a DataMill North 'cycle routes' layer from Durham County Council (inaccessible this session), or a request to activetravel@durham.gov.uk for audited network length. A GM equivalent would need TfGM Bee Network built-km data.

metrics.unavailable_reason: No third-party benchmark scores Durham County Council on a 0-100 scale. No Durham-specific rating was found in the coverage searched, and Durham does not appear in the 2015 top-20 list. The council's own Q4 2024-25 Corporate Performance Report (s211509) gives channel-shift data: non-digital contact is 58% now, against 77% before the pandemic. That is a single-dimension contact-channel share, not a composite adoption index. Building a composite from it would mean inventing a methodology, which is ruled out.

metrics.unavailable_reason: Durham does not report the share of major capital projects delivered on schedule. The annual capital outturn reports (FY2015-16 to FY2024-25, all opened) report spend against budget by service grouping, plus year-end reprofiling and additions/deletions in £m, with narrative on individual scheme slippage. There is no project-count or on-time/RAG share. A text search of all ten outturn reports and the Q4 2024-25 Corporate Performance Report for 'on schedule', 'on programme', 'behind schedule', 'RAG' and 'delivered on time' found no such measure. The performance report's procurement dashboard lists capital spend on four named projects, with no schedule status. metrics.unavailable_reason: No median days-to-approval figure is published for building or business permits. (1) Durham Building Control Customer Service Standards (durham.gov.uk article 2806) publishes only targets: contact within 15 working days of validation, a decision within statutory limits, and a fee refund if there is no decision within 25 working days or 2 months by agreement. It publishes no actual results. (2) The Building Safety Regulator's Operational Standards Rules monitoring arrangements (KPIs 1-6) contain no median or average decision-time KPI; the nearest, KPI 1.5, is the share of applications assessed within 5 weeks. The guidance does not show per-authority publication. Building control in England is also partly delivered by private registered building control approvers, so council data would not cover all permits. (3) Licensing: Durham's Q4 2024-25 performance report covers selective licensing coverage (52% of about 29,000 private rented properties fully licensed), which is not a processing time. Planning decision speed is covered under planning_efficiency_index and is a different instrument.

No 0-100 composite of planning throughput against caseload exists for Durham or any English LPA. The MHCLG live planning tables publish P151 (speed of major decisions: % decided within 13 weeks or agreed time, by LPA, rolling 24 months), P152 (quality of major decisions: % overturned at appeal), P153 (speed of non-major decisions: % within 8 weeks or agreed time) and PS1/PS2 open data (counts of applications received and decided, by quarter). These are percent-on-time and count measures, not a composite index. Turning them into a 0-100 index would mean inventing weights. Durham's own Q4 2024-25 Corporate Performance Report quotes the same series: 77% of major applications within 13 weeks (13 of 17) and 86% of non-major within deadline (311 of 363) in Jan-Mar 2025. If Mandate defines a percent-on-time metric, the MHCLG P151/P153 series is reproducible for both Durham (E06000047) and the GM LPAs.
metrics.caveats: MHCLG P151/P153/PS1/PS2 are a ready, GM-reproducible source for a separate 'planning decisions on time (%)' metric.

metrics.unavailable_reason: No published statistic gives Durham's median days from tender issue to contract award. metrics.unavailable_reason: No published series for County Durham measures RENTAL vacancy (vacant-for-rent units / total rental inventory, the ACS B25004 concept). Searched: (1) MHCLG Live Table 615 (Live_Table_615.ods, opened). Its sheets are All_vacants (County Durham 2024: 8,953), All_long_term_vacants (2024: 4,182), LA_owned_vacants (0 since Durham's 2015 stock transfer), PRP_general_needs_vacants (2024: 709), PRP_gen_needs_vacant_not_avail and Other_public_sector_vacants. All of these count whole-stock or social-landlord vacancy. None isolates private-rented vacancy, and none uses a rental-inventory denominator. A PRP-only rate would leave out the private rented sector, roughly half of rental stock (the selective licensing papers put the PRS at about 69,000 homes, of which about 29,000 are licensed at 42%). (2) Durham's 2011 Private Sector Housing Strategy report (Wayback copy) gives only 'over 4,000 private sector homes empty 6+ months' from council tax data. 'Private sector' means owner-occupied plus private rented, the date is outside the range, and it is long-term empties, not vacant-for-rent. (3) Selective licensing papers: the 25 Feb 2025 OSC update report and the 22 Apr 2024 OSC report (both Wayback copies) contain no vacancy figure. The 2020 designation evidence (s117584 report, s117586 Appendix A data) has no Wayback capture, and democracy.durham.gov.uk refuses HTTPS from this machine. Search snippets show only council-tax 'private sector' empties, not a PRS vacancy rate. (4) Empty Homes appendix and LHNA material found by search give whole-stock void rates (e.g. 4.1% of all stock). (5) The English Housing Survey is England-only, and Census 2021 unoccupied-dwelling counts carry no tenure. Whole-stock vacancy is explicitly not an acceptable substitute, so the gap is genuine. The same national sources apply to GM, so this would also be unavailable there.
metrics.caveats: This confirms the earlier judgment. Closest proxies, all a different concept: MHCLG table 615 whole-stock vacancy, and PRP social-landlord general-needs vacancy, which is social rented only and has no PRS component. Neither may be shown as a rental vacancy rate.
metrics.precedent_match: No GM precedent. The constraint is the same nationally (table 615 and EHS are identical sources for GM), so GM would also be unavailable on this definition.

metrics.unavailable_reason: No single-night point-in-time count of sheltered AND unsheltered individuals exists for County Durham. What exists: (1) MHCLG Rough Sleeping Snapshot (autumn, 2010-2024 LA tables, opened). It covers unsheltered people only, on one night between 1 Oct and 30 Nov, and explicitly excludes hostels, shelters and TA. Durham's figures are an 'Estimate' or 'Estimate including spotlight' (Table 3), not a street count. Table_1_Total, County Durham row: 2015=3, 2016=12, 2017=13, 2018=12, 2019=2, 2020=11, 2021=11, 2022=8, 2023=11, 2024=18. (2) MHCLG H-CLIC statutory homelessness detailed LA tables (Detailed_LA_202506, opened). Prevention and relief duties are household flows over a quarter. TA1 is a stock count of HOUSEHOLDS in temporary accommodation at quarter end, plus the number of children: Durham at 30 Jun 2025 had 146 households, 67 with children, 142 children. Adults are not counted, so individuals cannot be derived. (3) The Crisis/Heriot-Watt Homelessness Monitor 'core homelessness' is a modeled national estimate of households, includes sofa-surfing and has no published Durham figure. Combining the TA1 stock with the rough-sleeping snapshot would still differ from a PIT count. It would mix households (TA) with individuals (rough sleepers). It would mix different nights (quarter-end 30 Jun, 30 Sep, 31 Dec or 31 Mar against an autumn snapshot night). It would miss people in non-statutory hostels and supported housing outside TA. And the TA count includes households placed in TA outside the district. That would be a force-fit, so the status is unavailable.
metrics.caveats: This confirms the earlier judgment. The rough sleeping snapshot values above are given only as documentation of the unsheltered-only alternative. They must not be loaded as homelessness_count.
metrics.precedent_match: No GM precedent. The same national series (snapshot, H-CLIC) apply to GM, so it would also be unavailable on the sheltered+unsheltered PIT definition.

metrics.unavailable_reason: No published MEDIAN calendar days from application to decision for Durham. (1) MHCLG Planning applications in England (Apr-Jun 2026 release, opened) publishes only percentage-within-time measures (P151-P155 and others). The release confirms there is no average or median time to decision. Scotland and NI publish average weeks, England does not. (2) planning.data.gov.uk planning-application dataset (API queried): 0 records for Durham County Council (organisation entity 114). (3) North East Connected article of 29 Sep 2025 (opened). It reports a Travis Perkins FOI to Durham covering 2022-2024 (6,411 applications: 331 major, 1,810 minor, 4,270 other). It gives only 'average decision times' by category as ranges ('major up to 51 weeks (2023)', 'minor 16-22 weeks', 'other 11-15 weeks') and one outlier of 2,176 days. It does not state mean or median, gives no year-by-category table and no overall figure, and links no primary FOI response. The Sunderland Echo version and WhatDoTheyKnow were blocked by Cloudflare (403). No FOI response is published on a Durham disclosure log that I could find. Even with the primary response, per-category means cannot be combined into an all-applications median. (4) Durham quarterly performance reports and search results show only % within statutory or agreed time. Commercial aggregators (planningsignal: 'average 62 days, last 24 months', page timed out; planwatch: no figures) are not primary, give no year series, and use unknown method or validation dates. A median could in principle be built from Durham's own Idox public register (received/validated date to decision date) as a new derived dataset, but none is published.
metrics.caveats: This confirms the earlier judgment. MHCLG's % decided within statutory or agreed time is a different concept, and agreed extensions make it diverge sharply from elapsed days. The Travis Perkins FOI category averages are mean-or-unspecified, given as ranges, and secondary-reported, so they are not usable as a median.
metrics.precedent_match: No GM precedent. MHCLG publishes no time-to-decision for any English LPA, so GM's ten LPAs would also be unavailable. A future reproducible route for both would be computing medians from each LPA's planning register, or from planning.data.gov.uk once the LPAs publish there.

issues: I re-derived every figure the researcher quoted and all of them match the primary tables. The researcher missed a named, published, LA-level source that measures the target concept: Shelter's annual 'Homelessness in England' reports. Each estimates the number of PEOPLE (adults plus children) recorded as homeless on a given night, for every English local authority. The components are (a) people in council-arranged TA, converting households to persons using MHCLG TA2 household composition, with 'other' households assumed to be 2 people, (b) people in self-arranged TA or homeless at home, from TA1 'duty owed, no accommodation secured' times the regional average TA household size, and (c) rough sleepers from the MHCLG autumn snapshot. This answers two of the researcher's force-fit objections: the households-versus-individuals problem (Shelter converts to persons) and the 'no published Durham figure' problem (Durham rows are published).

Why the status is estimated and not real: the figures are modelled conversions of household counts to persons. MANDATE DURHAM SWEEP: COMPLETENESS AND CONSISTENCY CRITIC

MISSING

None. All 20 metrics have a final status:
- Real (4): transit_ridership, transit_reliability, average_commute_minutes, active_transportation_mode_share.
- Estimated (6): violent_crime_rate and property_crime_rate (both downgraded by the verifier), clearance_rate, emergency_response_minutes, capital_budget_execution_rate, public_transport_expansion_miles.
- Unavailable (10): bike_infrastructure_miles, agency_vacancy_rate, digital_government_adoption, major_infrastructure_delivery_rate, permit_approval_days, planning_efficiency_index, procurement_timeline_days, vacancy_rate, planning_approval_days, homelessness_count. homelessness_count is disputed: the verifier proposes estimated with Shelter rows (see Human decisions).

Gaps inside covered metrics:
- capital_budget_execution_rate has no FY2025-26 row. Report s226092 exists, but there is no Wayback copy and democracy.durham.gov.uk refuses connections from this machine. It needs a manual pull.
- transit_reliability has no FY2021-22 row, because DfT shows [z] for that year.
- transit_ridership ends at FY2024-25. The next DfT release is November 2026.
- average_commute_minutes has only two points (2015 and 2016).
- The proposed Shelter homelessness rows have no 2020 row.

CONSISTENCY ISSUES

1. Mixed geography within Public Safety. Two areas are in use:
   - violent_crime_rate and property_crime_rate use the County Durham CSP, which is the council area (E06000047).
   - clearance_rate uses the Durham Constabulary force area (County Durham plus Darlington). emergency_response_minutes uses the County Durham and Darlington fire authority area.

   So clearance is computed over a wider offence base than the crime rates beside it. Every row discloses this, and no council-level source exists. For contrast, all GM rows are force or authority level, which equals the GMCA area, so GM is internally consistent and Durham is not.

2. Population denominators for the crime rates.
   - FY2015-16 to FY2019-20 (derived): uses the original-vintage ONS mid-year estimate, taken from the year two before the financial year ends. This matches the ONS PFA table convention.
   - FY2020-21 to FY2025-26 (ONS-published): each row uses its own edition's vintage.
   - Exception: FY2024-25 uses mid-2022 (528,100). By the convention it should use mid-2023, which is what the force-level P3 table and GM's FY2024-25 row use. On mid-2023 the values would be about 3,406 violent instead of 3,443, roughly 1% lower, and property would fall by a similar amount.
   - The derived rows use Home Office counts revised in July 2026. The published rows use counts as first published. The difference is negligible (for example 20,848 vs 20,849).

3. Fiscal-year labelling. This is consistent: every uk_fiscal_year metric uses FYyyyy-yy with period_start on April 1, and the "year ending March YYYY" to FY(YYYY-1) mapping was verified for the DfT bus tables. The problem is across jurisdictions. GM's transit_ridership is calendar 2024 and GM's transit_reliability is labelled "2025" for a single month, while Durham uses uk_fiscal_year for both. Within one metric, the two jurisdictions sit on different period types.

4. Mixed period types and reference dates (disclosed, acceptable):
   - Commute: the LFS asks only in October to December, but rows are labelled as the calendar year with period_start January 1.
   - Census mode share: census day is in March, but rows start January 1.
   - Shelter homelessness: the reference date is 31 March for 2018 and 2019 and 30 June from 2021, so there is a break inside the series.

5. Units.
   - Crime per 100,000 as integers: OK.
   - All percentages are on a 0 to 100 scale: OK.
   - Fire response in decimal minutes: OK.
   - transit_ridership is stored as absolute journeys (for example 22,111,604). Check that GM's Metrolink row is also stored as journeys, not millions.

6. Vocabulary that may break the importer. The verifier's Shelter rows use confidence "modeled", data_quality "alternative" and source_type "advocacy_report". No other batch uses these values. Confirm the importer and schema accept them before any import.

7. Status labels within a metric. violent_crime_rate and property_crime_rate now mix row confidence "high" (ONS-published) with "estimated" (derived) under a metric-level status of estimated. That is consistent with the rule, but the same metric is "government" for GM.

COMPARABILITY ISSUES WITH GREATER MANCHESTER

Divergences that are disclosed but still produce a non-comparable pair:
- **transit_ridership:** Durham is bus only (DfT BUS01e), financial year, status real. GM is Metrolink only, calendar 2024, status estimated. A side-by-side compares buses with trams. GM's BUS01e row exists (171.04m for FY2024-25).
- **transit_reliability:** Durham is BUS09a, non-frequent services only, financial year, reported by the council. GM is TfGM whole-network on-time, March 2025 only. GM's BUS09a row exists (73 for FY2024-25).
- **emergency_response_minutes:** Durham is the mean response to primary fires from Home Office FIRE1001. GM's 7.35 is GMFRS's internal life-risk composite. On the FIRE1001 basis GM is 7.22 for primary fires (6.65 for dwellings). GM's 7.35 is also a mean but carries "government", while Durham's equivalent is "estimated". That is a status inconsistency in the existing GM row.
- **capital_budget_execution_rate:**
  - Denominator: Durham uses the latest Cabinet-approved revised budget, GM the latest forecast. Both are estimated, so this is acceptable.
  - Scope, not disclosed: Durham is General Fund capital only. The GMCA programme's scope (transport, fire and so on) is not stated against it.
  - Entity, not disclosed: a combined authority is being compared with a unitary council.

Divergences not flagged as GM differences:
- **Crime status gap:** violent_crime_rate and property_crime_rate will show "estimated" for Durham and "government" for GM on the same metric, purely because of the five derived pre-2020 rows. The cause is the derivation, not a concept difference, and a reader will not see that.
- **FY2024-25 population vintage:** Durham FY2024-25 crime uses mid-2022 while GM FY2024-25 uses mid-2023, a gap of about 1%.
- **Year coverage in the crime series:** Durham has a full FY2019-20 crime row. GM has none (GMP IT gap). This is harmless, but year-by-year charts will have an unmatched point.
